segments.voice: Chapter five of the Gita opens with a student losing patience. Arjuna has heard Krishna praise two things that sound like opposites. On one side, giving up action, setting it all down. On the other, action done as yoga, work done without grabbing at its fruit. Which is it? Arjuna wants one answer, stated plainly. Krishna does answer him. But the answer turns the question inside out.
screen: `TWO ANSWERS. PICK ONE.` → `ARJUNA WANTS IT PLAIN.` → `THE ANSWER TURNS THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Here's Krishna's reply, in paraphrase. Both roads, renouncing action and the yoga of action, lead to the highest good. But of the two, the yoga of action is the better. Then he says who the real renouncer is: the one who neither hates nor craves. Not the person who has left the house. The person who has stopped pushing and pulling inside. A verse or two later he goes further. Only children, he says, talk about the way of knowing and the way of action as two separate things. The one who sees them as one, sees. The person who knows the truth, Krishna says, thinks: I am not really the doer of anything. And he lists the day as it happens. Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing, speaking, letting go, taking hold, opening and closing the eyes. All the while, that person holds that the senses are simply moving among their objects. The commentators read this chapter differently. Shankara, the teacher of non-duality, reads true renunciation as belonging with knowledge of the Self, and action without attachment as the ground that makes that knowledge possible. Ramanuja reads the way of action as an easier road to walk, one that already carries knowledge inside it. This is why Hinduism honors two lives. A few take sannyasa, the renouncer's vow: the ochre cloth, no home, no possessions. Most stay householders, with jobs and families. Krishna's line means the householder isn't second best: whoever stops hating and craving is, in his words, always a renouncer. So karma here isn't a ledger of rewards and punishments. It's the doing nobody escapes, and who we take to be doing it.
screen: `BOTH ROADS LEAD TO THE GOOD.` · `THE RENOUNCER NEITHER HATES NOR CRAVES.` · `SEEING, HEARING, BREATHING: I DO NOTHING.` · `SHANKARA AND RAMANUJA, SAME VERSES.` · `MONK OR HOUSEHOLDER: THE SAME GOAL.` · then, large: `WHO IS DOING THE DOING?`

segments.voice: Go through Krishna's list slowly, as it happens in you right now: seeing, hearing whatever sound is in the room, touching the chair, breathing, the eyes closing. Don't try to stop any of it; just notice how much is being done without any effort from you at all. If you pray, you can rest in that noticing as your prayer; if not, simply watch the senses move among their objects.
Karma. Action, the plain fact of doing. In chapter five, the question isn't whether to act, but who we take to be acting.

968.title: The lotus leaf in the water
968.hook: a lotus leaf sits in the water all day and comes out dry

968.howItsDone: Many Hindu families close a puja by offering all their actions to God, with the Bhagavata Purana's prayer 'kayena vacha...' or simply 'Krishnarpanamastu', and teachers point to the Gita's lotus leaf when they speak about working in the world without clinging to its results.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma in chapter five: Krishna's list of seeing, hearing, walking, breathing, and the knower who thinks, the real renouncer neither hates nor craves.
screen: `KARMA.` · `SEEING, HEARING, WALKING, BREATHING.`

segments.voice: A lotus leaf spends its whole life in a pond. Rain lands on it, water laps at its edges, and still, lift it out and the surface is dry. The Gita takes that ordinary sight and makes it the picture for a whole way of acting.
screen: `A LEAF IN THE POND ALL DAY.` → `LIFT IT OUT: DRY.` → `A WHOLE WAY OF ACTING.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. The one who acts, setting every action in Brahman and letting go of attachment, isn't stained by wrongdoing, the way a lotus leaf isn't wet by water. The leaf doesn't leave the pond or hide from the rain. It's in the water completely, and the water doesn't cling. Chapter three starts from a plain fact: nobody can stay even a moment without acting. Even keeping the body going is action. Chapter four turns the screw: the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction. Someone can sit perfectly still and be churning inside, and someone can work all day and be at rest. Then chapter five gives us the leaf. The next verses say the yogis act with body, mind and understanding, even with the senses alone, letting go of attachment, to make themselves clean. The one who lets go of the fruit comes to a steady peace, while the one who grabs at the fruit, driven by wanting, is bound. The commentators agree on the leaf and differ on the phrase before it: is setting an act in Brahman handing it to the Lord, as a servant works for a master, or seeing that nature, not the Self, does the work? Many Hindu families live this verse without naming it. At the end of a puja they say an old prayer from the Bhagavata Purana: whatever I do, with body, speech, mind or senses, I offer it all to Narayana. Some say it in one word: Krishnarpanamastu, let it be offered to Krishna. That's karma yoga in a breath: do the work all the way, hand over the fruit, and praise or blame rolls off like water.
screen: `THE LEAF STAYS IN THE WATER.` · `CHAPTER THREE: NOBODY STOPS ACTING.` · `CHAPTER FOUR: STILLNESS INSIDE THE WORK.` · `CHAPTER FIVE: OFFER IT, AND STAY DRY.` · `KRISHNARPANAMASTU: LET IT BE OFFERED.` · then, large: `IN THE WATER, NOT WET.`

segments.voice: Hold your hands open, palms up, like two leaves, and let the day's water come: a waiting task, a conversation still running in your head. Let it land, and with each out-breath feel it bead up and roll away while the hands stay where they are. If you pray, you can set one of today's tasks in the hands of the one you pray to as you breathe out, the way families say Krishnarpanamastu, let it be offered to Krishna.
Karma. Action, the work no one can step out of. In the Gita's lotus leaf, it's work done fully, with nothing clinging to it.

969.hook: twice the Gita describes people near the goal as delighting in the good of all beings

segments.voice: Sarvabhutahite ratah. A short Sanskrit phrase that turns up twice in the Gita, both times describing people who've come close to the goal. It means delighting in the good of all beings. Over six days, we'll sketch a year of service. Today, the reason under the whole thing.
screen: `TWICE IN THE GITA.` → `DELIGHTING IN THE GOOD OF ALL BEINGS.` → `SIX DAYS: A YEAR OF SERVICE.`

segments.voice: First, in paraphrase: near the end of chapter five, Krishna describes the sages who reach the peace of Brahman: their faults worn away, their doubts cut through, their selves held steady, delighting in the good of all beings. Then, in chapter twelve, Arjuna asks which worshipers know yoga better: those who love God with a form, or those who seek the imperishable, beyond form? Krishna answers that those who fix their minds on him are the most devoted. But of the second group he says: with the senses held in, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the good of all beings, they too come to me. The phrase sits not in a chapter on charity, not in a list of rules, but inside portraits of people near the end of the path. On this reading, care for others isn't only a road toward the goal. It's one of the marks of having come close to it. That gives seva, a word Hindus use for service, a particular root. Not service as an extra on a free weekend but as something a settled heart is glad to do. And look at the word all. Not all who agree with me, not all in my family or my town. All beings. Hindu homes have an old way of practicing that word. The law books list five daily offerings a householder makes, and one of them is to the beings: a little food set out for birds, animals, whatever lives nearby. It's why some grandmothers put out rice for the birds, or the first roti for a cow, before the family eats. A temple kitchen feeding whoever walks in is the same idea, bigger. So a year of service can start before any calendar: whose good would you be glad to see, and how far past your own people can that circle reach?
screen: `CHAPTER FIVE: THE SAGES NEAR THE GOAL.` · `CHAPTER TWELVE: THE SAME PHRASE.` · `CARE AS A MARK OF COMING CLOSE.` · `FOOD FOR THE BIRDS BEFORE BREAKFAST.` · then, large: `ALL BEINGS, NOT SOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose good you'd be glad to see today, then let the circle open one ring at a time, a neighbor, a coworker, a stranger in another city, an animal, a tree on your street, and notice where gladness gets harder, marking that place without pushing past it. If you pray, you can hold the whole circle before the one you pray to.

970.title: Better your own dharma
970.hook: better your own work done imperfectly than someone else's done well
970.carry: better your own dharma, done imperfectly
970.howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Gita's svadharma verses in more than one way, some tying them to caste and stage of life and others to a person's nature and situation; some people turn to the verse when weighing what kind of work or service is theirs.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first piece of a year of service designed: sarvabhutahite ratah, delighting in the good of all beings.

segments.voice: Somebody online is rebuilding houses after a flood. Somebody else runs a soup kitchen, fosters dogs, teaches kids to read. It's inspiring, and it can also leave a person frozen, scrolling through other people's good work and wondering whether their own is too small to count. The Gita has a verse for that exact paralysis. Krishna says it in chapter three, and nearly again near the end of the book. Today: which service is actually yours.
screen: `OTHER PEOPLE'S GOOD WORK.` → `FROZEN, SCROLLING.` → `WHICH SERVICE IS YOURS?`

segments.voice: In paraphrase: better your own dharma, even done imperfectly, than the dharma of another done well. The word is svadharma. Sva means one's own. Dharma is a big word, duty, right order, the way a thing is meant to work; here it's the duty that belongs to your actual place in life. In the Gita's story, Arjuna is a warrior who has just said he'd rather live as a beggar than fight, and Krishna is telling him not to trade his own hard task for someone else's that looks easier or holier. In chapter eighteen the line comes back: by doing the work that belongs to your own nature, you don't incur fault. There it comes right after verses on the duties of the four varnas, the classes of the old social order, each said to arise from its own nature. Hindu readers have argued about how to apply that. Older readings tie svadharma to varna, caste, and stage of life. Some modern Hindu teachers read it more as the duty that fits your nature, your gifts, your situation, and that reading has its critics too. And notice the word imperfectly. Krishna isn't promising your service will be impressive. He's saying it will be yours. So the first question changes: not what's the most admirable work out there, but what's mine to do. The parent of a small child may have a year of service that looks like patience at bedtime and one shift a month somewhere else. A nurse might serve by not cutting corners on a tired night. Someone with a car might be the one who drives. The flood houses are real and good. They just might belong to someone else.
screen: `BETTER YOUR OWN, DONE IMPERFECTLY.` · `SVADHARMA: THE DUTY THAT IS YOURS.` · `READERS HAVE ARGUED OVER HOW TO APPLY IT.` · `NOT ADMIRABLE: MINE TO DO.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MINE TO DO?`

segments.voice: Let three things come up without judging them: something you're simply good at; a place you're already in, a group, a route you drive; and a person who already relies on you. Breathe with each and see where the three overlap, since that overlap may be the start of your own dharma of service, imperfect and yours. If you pray, you can ask the one you pray to for clarity about it.
Svadharma. One's own dharma, the service that belongs to your own life, better done imperfectly than another's done well.

971.title: The three kinds of gift
971.hook: the Gita sorts gifts into three kinds, and only one needs no thank-you
971.carry: the sattvic gift expects nothing back
971.howItsDone: Dana, giving, is part of Hindu practice at festivals, temple visits and family occasions, and some Hindus point to the Gita's description of the sattvic gift, given without expecting return, when they talk about how to give.

segments.voice: A twenty-dollar bill can be three completely different gifts. Handed over with a little speech about how generous this is. Pushed across the table with a sigh, because saying no would be awkward. Or slipped to the right person, at the right moment, with no one keeping score. In chapter seventeen of the Gita, Arjuna asks about people who worship with faith but outside the scriptures' rules. Krishna answers by sorting faith, food, sacrifice and discipline by the three gunas, the qualities that run through everything, and giving gets three verses. Same bill, three gifts.
screen: `ONE BILL, THREE GIFTS.` → `CHAPTER SEVENTEEN SORTS THEM.` → `HOW TO GIVE.`

segments.voice: The gunas are sattva, clarity and balance; rajas, restless drive; and tamas, heaviness and dullness. Here are the three gifts, in paraphrase. The sattvic gift is given simply because giving is right, to someone who can do nothing in return, at the right place and time, to a fitting person. The rajasic gift is given to get something back, or with an eye to some reward, or grudgingly. The tamasic gift is given at the wrong place and time, to the wrong person, without respect, with contempt. Look at what the first gift asks for. Not size; the verse doesn't mention an amount at all. Four things: the right reason, which is that it's right; no return; the right timing; and the right person. That last part keeps it from being careless. Giving well takes attention. Who actually needs this? Is now the moment, or would next month be better for them? The second gift isn't evil. It's just tangled up with getting, and the Gita puts giving with reluctance in it, which is honest about how giving can feel. The third comes with contempt, so whatever it helps with, it also wounds. This is the measure many Hindus hold their own giving to, at a festival, a temple, a family occasion: not how much, but whether anything is expected back. Before you give, the Gita would have you ask four questions. Why am I giving? What am I expecting back? When is the right time? To whom? Dana, the gift, is part of Hindu practice. Chapter seventeen asks that it be done with clear eyes.

972.title: The guest as god
972.hook: a graduation speech in an Upanishad tells students to treat the guest as a god
972.carry: let the guest be a god to you
972.tomorrow: As hard to hold as the wind
972.howItsDone: Hospitality has a respected place in Hindu homes, and the Taittiriya Upanishad's line atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you, is a saying some families teach their children.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, dana: the gift sorted three ways, and four questions: the sattvic gift expects nothing back.
screen: `THE GIFT.` · `THE SATTVIC GIFT EXPECTS NOTHING BACK.`

segments.voice: Students are about to leave their teacher's house. Their study is done. Before they go, the teacher gives them a last talk, the kind of advice you'd hope to hear at any graduation. Speak the truth. Follow dharma. Don't neglect your study. Don't neglect your duty to the gods and the ancestors. Then comes a run of short lines that some Hindus still know by heart. That farewell talk sits in the Taittiriya Upanishad, and one of its lines gives today's piece of a year of service: the people who come through your door.
screen: `THE STUDENTS ARE LEAVING.` → `THE TEACHER'S LAST TALK.` → `THE PEOPLE AT YOUR DOOR.`

segments.voice: The run of lines goes like this, in paraphrase. Let your mother be a god to you. Let your father be a god to you. Let your teacher be a god to you. Let your guest be a god to you. In Sanskrit that last one is atithi devo bhava. Atithi is the guest. Devo bhava, be as a god. Notice who's on that list. Mother, father, teacher: people you owe something to, people who came first. And then the guest, who may be a stranger, someone you owe nothing at all. The Upanishad puts them in the same row. The same talk goes on to giving: give with faith, not without faith, give with modesty, give with understanding. So the teacher sets hospitality and giving side by side, as a life's practice rather than a one-time act. In a year of service, this may be the piece closest to home. A spare chair at the table. The colleague nobody invites to lunch. The new family on the street. A cousin in town for a hospital stay who needs a place to sleep. The tradition doesn't ask for a grand gesture. It asks for a door that opens, and for the person who walks through it to be received with the care you'd give to something holy. It's also one of the householder's five daily offerings from earlier this week: hospitality to people. Service that never has to leave home.
screen: `MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST AS A GOD.` · `HOSPITALITY AND GIVING, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `A DOOR THAT OPENS.` · then, large: `RECEIVE THEM AS HOLY.`

segments.voice: Picture your own front door, or the door of the room where you spend your days, and let one person come through it, someone likely to come by in the next few months: a neighbor, a coworker, a relative, a friend of your child. Notice how you'd usually greet them, then, without changing anything outward, let the greeting deepen inside, as if receiving someone who matters more than you knew. If you pray, you can see the one you pray to in that guest.
Atithi. The guest, the one the Upanishad says to receive as a god, let the guest be a god to you.

973.title: As hard to hold as the wind
973.hook: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Krishna agrees
973.carry: the mind is held by practice and letting go
973.tomorrow: a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water
973.howItsDone: Some Hindus keep service in a regular rhythm, such as a weekly shift in a temple kitchen or giving tied to festivals in the calendar, and teachers point to the Gita's pairing of abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go, for steadying the mind.

screen: `DAY NINE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, piece four of a year of service: the guest, atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you.
screen: `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA.` · `LET THE GUEST BE A GOD.`

segments.voice: Plans made in a quiet week have a way of dissolving once the busy weeks come back. Arjuna knew the problem from the inside. In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna has been describing a mind that rests even and steady, and Arjuna pushes back. The mind, he says, is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn. Holding it still seems to me as hard as holding the wind. It's a very human moment: that sounds lovely, but I don't think I can. And Krishna doesn't argue.
screen: `PLANS DISSOLVE IN BUSY WEEKS.` → `AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.` → `KRISHNA DOESN'T ARGUE.`

segments.voice: His answer, in paraphrase: no doubt, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held by abhyasa and vairagya. Abhyasa is practice, the same thing done again and again. Vairagya is letting go, loosening the grip of wanting. No secret technique. Just practice, and a looser hand. Look back over this week through that pair. We began with karma. In chapter five, the true renouncer neither hates nor craves, and the lotus leaf sits in the water all day without getting wet. That's vairagya: staying in the work, letting the results roll off. Then we started designing a year of service. Delight in the good of all beings gave the reason. Svadharma gave the where: your own service, done imperfectly. The gift gave four questions: why, what back, when, to whom. The guest gave the door. All of that is a design. What it still needs is abhyasa. A year of service isn't one big decision. It's a rhythm: one day a week, one evening a month, one gift each season, one meal shared when the calendar comes round. Abhyasa, on this reading, is more about returning than about intensity. And vairagya keeps the rhythm from turning into a tally of hits and misses, because the day you miss, or the gift that goes unthanked, is just water on the leaf. Arjuna said the mind was like the wind. Krishna didn't say it wasn't. He said there's a way to hold it, and it looks a lot like showing up again.
screen: `ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA.` · `THIS WEEK: THE LEAF, ALL BEINGS, THE GIFT, THE GUEST.` · `A YEAR OF SERVICE IS A RHYTHM.` · `A MISSED DAY IS WATER ON THE LEAF.` · then, large: `SHOW UP AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Let the breath be the practice, in, out, again, and when the mind runs off, as it will, notice where it went and come back without scolding: abhyasa and vairagya in miniature. Then let this week's pieces come up one at a time, the leaf, the good of all beings, your own service, the gift, the guest, and ask of each one question, how often, letting a rhythm suggest itself. If you pray, you can offer that rhythm to the one you pray to.
Abhyasa. Practice that repeats, held together with vairagya, a loose hand on the results.
